description: Music Years 3-4 width tiers — ACARA v9. All strands are capability strands; width axis is task_contexts throughout.
subject: Music

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest single musical context that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For Y3-4, minimum is typically one activity type demonstrating the descriptor's key verb (manipulate, develop, explore, sing/play).
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope across the most common elaboration cases. Reflects a well-taught Y3-4 class engaging with a range of musical contexts, purposes and tools.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding new task contexts — different genres, cultural settings, technologies, purposes or ensemble types. First Nations contexts included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data. E02 descriptor is entirely First Nations-focused and its elaborations are the primary framing for that entry.

AC9AMU4C01.minimum_width: Manipulate at least two elements of music (e.g. dynamics and tempo) when composing or practising a piece that communicates a clear idea or mood; notate or record the work using any available format.
AC9AMU4C01.typical_width: Manipulate elements of music across multiple composition contexts — writing lyrics/melodies for songs or chants, using available technologies to create loop-based or digital accompaniments, improvising on known pitches and rhythms, manipulating dynamics and tempo to express character or dramatic action; use graphic notation, lead-sheets or audio recording to document work; work in pairs or groups to compose ostinatos or accompaniments.
wider: Compose music for a screen-based work or to accompany a drama (e.g. retelling a children's story) — manipulate elements to match characters and dramatic action
Learn and compose music associated with cultures from Asia or other specific cultural groups in the local community — draw on characteristic rhythmic patterns or melodic styles
Combine composed and improvised sections into a complete work (e.g. a composed melody with soundscape improvisations for a narrated story)
Use ukuleles, bucket drums or other classroom instruments to compose ostinatos or accompaniments in a small group — document using a combination of graphic and staff notation
elaborations: writing lyrics and/or melodies for songs, raps or chants and using formats such as graphic or staff notation or a lead-sheet or an audio recording to notate/document/record their work
using available technologies to create accompaniments; for example, improvising patterns and recording as a loop or using digital tools to notate/document music
improvising phrases of music on an instrument to practise known notes and rhythm patterns
learning songs and/or instrumental music associated with specific cultures
listening to live or recorded performances and gathering ideas they can use in their performance
manipulating the elements of music to express different characters or dramatic action when composing music for a screen-based work or to accompany drama
combining composed and improvised sections to create a complete work
working in pairs or groups to create ostinatos or accompaniments

AC9AMU4D01.minimum_width: Manipulate one element of music (e.g. dynamics or pitch) when singing or playing; describe the effect created and compare with a different approach.
AC9AMU4D01.typical_width: Develop listening skills and skills for manipulating elements of music across a range of singing and instrumental contexts — varying dynamics, combining different instruments for mood, using combinations of melodic steps and jumps; practise reading staff, graphic and/or invented notation; listen to diverse music examples to explore how rhythm, pitch and timbre are used; explore options for representing sounds in a score.
wider: Invent a graphic score to represent environmental sounds, then use the score in rehearsal — refine it for accuracy and ease of use in performance

Listen to examples from diverse musical traditions and compare how characteristic rhythmic or melodic patterns are used — identify whether patterns repeat across the whole work or only in specific sections
Develop ensemble listening skills through small-group performance — focus on blending dynamics and adjusting individual contributions in response to others
Use digital tools (loop software, notation apps) to create and document accompaniments — compare how digital and graphic notation convey different types of musical information
elaborations: using speaking, singing, voice/vocalisation and movement to develop skills for singing/vocalisation
manipulating elements of music to create and control intended effects, using sounds from a range of sources
singing and playing learnt pitch and rhythm patterns and varying elements of music within them to create different effects
listening to the effects they create by manipulating elements of music in different ways
listening to diverse examples of music to explore how rhythm and pitch patterns, structures or timbres are used
practising reading staff, graphic and/or invented notation as they rehearse and perform
exploring options for representing sounds in a score

AC9AMU4E01.minimum_width: Listen to music created for one specific purpose (e.g. a dance, a ceremony or a storytelling song) and share one observation about how elements of music serve that purpose.
AC9AMU4E01.typical_width: Explore where, why and how music is composed and performed across cultures, times and places — comparing music for similar purposes across different contexts; examining music performed by local choirs or cultural groups; comparing performance expectations and audience behaviours in different settings; exploring different notation and documentation forms; exploring instrument-making from recycled/repurposed materials.
wider: Compare music created for similar purposes (e.g. dance music or songs that communicate identity) across different historical periods or cultural contexts — focus on how elements of music are used in each
Investigate a local choir or cultural group's music — attend a performance or access a recording, then respond by describing what you like, find interesting or want to know more about
Explore different ways of notating music (graphic notation, lead-sheets, staff notation) and explain how each format conveys different information to performers
Construct instruments from recycled/repurposed materials — use them to create Foley sounds or a soundscape for an exhibition or presentation, linking instrument design to musical purpose
elaborations: exploring examples of music created for similar purposes across different times and/or places, such as music for dancing, songs that communicate messages, or narrative songs
examining the purpose for which music is used in their lives and community
comparing the expectations and requirements of performers and audiences in different performance settings
exploring ways of notating or documenting forms of music
exploring ways to make instruments from a range of materials

AC9AMU4E02.minimum_width: Listen to one example of music by First Nations Australians that communicates connection to Country/Place; identify at least one way the music communicates this connection.
AC9AMU4E02.typical_width: Explore how First Nations Australians use music to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place — listening to songs with lyrics about Country/Place, music accompanying dances that communicate knowledge, interviews/podcasts by First Nations musicians; learn about expectations and requirements for performers and audiences experiencing culturally significant music.
wider: Use resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians (interviews, podcasts, performances) to learn how composers and performers describe their relationship to Country/Place through music
Listen to and discuss music used during a Welcome to Country or other community ceremony — explore the protocols and responsibilities involved for performers and audiences

Compare two or more examples of First Nations Australian music communicating connection to Country/Place — explore how different songwriters or performers use elements of music differently to convey similar themes
elaborations: examining a diverse range of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians to communicate connection to, and responsibility for Country/Place
listening to and exploring music that shares feelings and ideas about the importance of Country/Place and Story for First Nations Australians
learning from First Nations Australians about how they use music to communicate their connection to, and responsibility for Country/Place, culture and people
learning from First Nations Australians about the expectations and requirements of performers and audiences experiencing music that communicates connection to Country/Place

AC9AMU4P01.minimum_width: Perform one piece of music (unison song, round or instrumental work) they have learnt or composed; introduce it by sharing one intended purpose or compositional decision.
AC9AMU4P01.typical_width: Sing and play music in informal settings — performing unison songs, rounds and ensemble music with melody and accompaniment parts; introduce performances by sharing compositional intent and how elements of music were used; rehearse and perform using a range of technologies (PA, microphones, recordings of rehearsals); plan staging and introduction formats for performances; read from notation or lead-sheets.
wider: Rehearse a performance using sound reinforcement equipment (PA, microphones, foldback) and adjust the setup to ensure audience and performers can hear each other clearly
Record rehearsals, listen back critically and make documented adjustments before a final performance — practise iterative refinement through listening
Plan and present a performance for a specific audience beyond the classroom (e.g. a school assembly, a community event) and reflect on how the context shaped the performance decisions
Present a performance of music associated with a specific cultural context, sharing information about the cultural significance of the music with the audience
elaborations: performing music such as unison songs, rounds and instrumental music arranged for small ensembles
introducing performances by sharing information such as the intended purposes of their compositions
rehearsing and performing music using a range of technologies
planning how they will stage a performance and introduce their performances to audiences
reading from notation and/or documentation such as a lead-sheet, staff or graphic notation when practising and performing
